President Trump took his midterm campaign blitz to the battleground state of Georgia yesterday.
He spoke on behalf of Republican candidates,
including Representative Mike Collins, who was running for U.S. Senate.
Trump also attacked Democratic Senator John Ossoff and former President Biden.
And from the moment John Ossoff became your senator,

A federal appeals court in Washington threw tough questions at the Justice Department
at a hearing yesterday about the Presidential Records Act. As NPR's Kerry Johnson reports,
the Trump administration is trying to invalidate the nearly 50-year-old law.
Congress passed the Records Act in 1978 after a tug of war over the papers of President Richard
Nixon. Since then, every White House has mostly complied with the law until now.
The Trump DOJ told the appeals court the law's an unconstitutional intrusion on the presidency.
The Justice Department argues the president's papers belong to him,
not the American people, as the law dictates. But Judges Patricia Millett and Cornelia Pillard
jumped in with skeptical questions about the need for future presidents to know about potential
national security threats. Historians and watchdogs have sued over the Trump move.
The case could eventually end up at the U.S. Supreme Court. Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
Fire crews in Southern California continue to battle a wildfire in San Juan Capistrano.
The battle to contain the fire is taking place on the ground and from the air,
with helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft dropping water and fire retardant on hot spots.
The biggest problem for firefighters are powerful Santa Ana winds,
which are pushing flames in different directions.
Naomi Jones' home was not damaged, but she was still shaken.
To see the whole neighborhood, it's heartbreaking.
Orange County Fire Captain Steve Consialdi says it could take some time before the danger is over.
We'll be here for a number of days protecting all the homes.
The winds are expected to continue during the weekend, but they should be less intense.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in San Juan Capistrano, California.
This is NPR. A new report by the Vatican says the number of Catholics in Africa has surpassed
Europe for the first time ever. Officials say Africa also recorded the highest worldwide
increase in the number of Catholics. NPR's Joelle Bright has that story.
The report by the Vatican's Fidesse News Agency says Africa's Catholic population
grew by over 7 million to 288 million by June 2024, slightly ahead of Europe's 287 million.
Globally, the Catholic Church's population stands at 1.4 billion,
representing around 17% of the global population. The Americas remain home to the largest population
of Catholics globally, with over 600 million faithful. The report also recorded a slight
increase in the number of priests worldwide, but there was a decline in the number of Catholic
women's religious groups and major seminarians. Joelle Bright, NPR News, Vegas.
Authorities say a Florida man has been charged with the murder of his former fiancee,
who went missing nearly 15 years ago. Orlando police say the murder happened after the two
appeared together in a pre-recorded episode of the show "The People's Court." Dale Smith Jr.
has been charged with second-degree murder. The body of his ex-fiancee, Michelle Parker,
has not been recovered, but police say all evidence leads to Smith as the person believed
to be responsible for her death. Smith is also being held without bond, pending a detention
hearing. I'm Lyndi Kenyon, NPR News. This message comes from Lisa and their lineup
